renders._yaml:
- component: figure
  title: Mapping efficiency per library
  description: |-
    Each bar is a library: the percentage of read pairs Bismark aligned to a unique best position. It answers which libraries mapped poorly.
    How to read: libraries of one experiment usually sit in a narrow band. A library far below the others points to the wrong reference genome, untrimmed adapters or a poor library, so check the trimming report and the Bismark FAQ on low mapping before using it.
    Note: Bismark publishes no mapping-efficiency cut-off.
    Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median mapping efficiency of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of Bismark.
    Source: https://felixkrueger.github.io/Bismark/faq/low-mapping/
  visu_type: bar
  dict_kwargs:
    x: sample
    y: mapping_efficiency_pct
    color: sample
    labels:
      sample: Library
      mapping_efficiency_pct: Mapping efficiency (%)
  reference_lines:
  - axis: y
    stat: median
    column: mapping_efficiency_pct

- component: card
  title: Average mapping efficiency
  description: |-
    The hero number is the mean percentage of read pairs aligned uniquely, and the box shows the spread across libraries. It answers how well the run mapped overall.
    How to read: a tight box means libraries behaved alike. A long lower whisker is a library to open in the bar chart.
  column: mapping_efficiency_pct
  aggregation: average
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: Mapping efficiency, with its spread

- component: card
  title: Weakest mapping efficiency
  description: |-
    The hero number is the lowest mapping efficiency of any library, shown with the median and the highest. It answers how far the worst library is from the rest.
    How to read: a minimum close to the median means no library stands out. A wide gap marks a library to inspect.
    Note: Bismark publishes no mapping-efficiency cut-off, so no pass mark is drawn.
    Source: https://felixkrueger.github.io/Bismark/faq/low-mapping/
  column: mapping_efficiency_pct
  aggregation: min
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: compact
  caption: Weakest library, with the median and the best

- component: card
  title: Read pairs analysed
  description: |-
    The hero number is the total of read pairs Bismark analysed, and the histogram shows how they spread over libraries. It answers whether sequencing depth is even.
    How to read: a narrow histogram means even depth. A long tail is a library with far more or fewer pairs than its peers.
  column: pairs_analysed
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: histogram
  caption: Read pairs per library

- component: card
  title: Pairs with no alignment
  description: |-
    The hero number is the total of read pairs that never aligned, and the histogram shows the spread over libraries. It answers how much input was lost before methylation calling.
    How to read: a library with a far larger count than its peers has a mapping problem. Compare it with the mapping efficiency bar chart.
  column: no_alignment
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: histogram
  caption: Unaligned pairs per library

- component: table
  title: Alignment table
  description: |-
    Each row is a library with the read pairs Bismark analysed, the unique best hits, the mapping efficiency and the pairs that did not align or were not unique. It answers the exact counts behind the bar chart.
    How to read: sort by mapping efficiency to find the weakest library, then compare its unaligned and non-unique counts.

- component: advanced_viz
  id: methylation_track
  title: Methylation along the genome
  description: |-
    Each trace is a library: the mean CpG methylation of every 10 kb window along a chromosome. It answers where methylation rises or drops, and whether libraries share the pattern.
    How to read: traces that move together show a shared methylome. A library that departs over a long stretch is a candidate for a copy-number change, a sex or cell-type difference, or a technical problem. Zoom to a chromosome to read the detail.
    Note: windows with too few CpGs in a library are dropped, so gaps are expected in CpG-poor regions.
  kind: coverage_track
  config:
    color_by: sample
  roles:
    chromosome: chromosome
    position: position
    value: methylation_pct
    end: end
    sample: sample

- component: advanced_viz
  id: methylation_genome_view
  title: Methylation genome view
  description: |-
    Each mark is a 10 kb window of a library, placed on the genome and coloured by library, with its mean CpG methylation as the height. It answers where along the genome methylation is high or low.
    How to read: compare libraries on the same region to spot a difference. Drag to select a region and open the windows in the table to read the exact values.
    Note: the window size is fixed at 10 kb, so smaller features, such as a single CpG island, are averaged out.
  kind: genome_view
  config:
    score_title: Methylation (%)
  roles:
    chr: chromosome
    pos: position
    score: methylation_pct
    end: end
    sample: sample

- component: card
  title: Average window methylation
  description: |-
    The hero number is the mean CpG methylation over all 10 kb windows, and the box shows how windows differ. It answers the overall methylation level and its spread.
    How to read: a box that reaches from low to high values is normal, since methylation varies by region. A shift of the whole box between libraries is a global difference.
  column: methylation_pct
  aggregation: average
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: Window methylation, with its spread

- component: card
  title: Median window methylation
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median CpG methylation of a window, drawn against the full 0 to 100 percent scale, with the lowest and highest window. It answers where the typical window sits.
    How to read: a median near the top is typical of mammalian somatic cells. A low median is typical of a hypomethylated sample or a conversion problem.
  column: methylation_pct
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - min
  - max
  secondary_layout: gauge
  coverage_max: 100.0
  caption: Median window methylation, out of 100%

- component: card
  title: CpGs by density class
  description: |-
    The hero number is the total of CpGs behind all windows, and the bar splits it by CpG density class. It answers how many CpGs sit in sparse and dense regions.
    How to read: the classes are tertiles of the CpG count per window, an annotation-free stand-in for CpG islands. Dense windows hold most of the CpGs.
  column: n_cpg
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: composition
  breakdown_col: cpg_density_class
  caption: CpGs, by density class

- component: card
  title: CpGs per window
  description: |-
    The hero number is the mean number of CpGs in a window, and the box shows the spread. It answers how much evidence sits behind each window mean.
    How to read: a window with few CpGs has a noisier methylation value. A wide box means windows differ strongly in density.
  column: n_cpg
  aggregation: average
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: CpGs per window, with their spread

- component: card
  title: Windows in the matrix
  description: |-
    The hero number is the count of library windows kept, and the histogram shows how their methylation spreads. It answers how many windows the genome view rests on and how bimodal they are.
    How to read: a histogram with peaks near the two ends is typical of methylation. A single peak in the middle suggests noise or poor conversion.
  column: methylation_pct
  aggregation: count
  aggregations:
  - min
  - max
  secondary_layout: histogram
  caption: Windows, with the methylation spread

- component: figure
  title: Methylation by CpG density
  description: |-
    Each box is the distribution of window methylation within one CpG density class. It answers whether CpG-dense windows are less methylated than sparse ones.
    How to read: methylation is typically lower in CpG-dense, island-like regions and higher in CpG-poor regions. A box that departs from this pattern points to a conversion problem or an unusual sample.
    Note: the classes are tertiles of the CpG count per window, not an island annotation.
  visu_type: box
  dict_kwargs:
    x: cpg_density_class
    y: methylation_pct
    color: cpg_density_class
    labels:
      cpg_density_class: CpG density class
      methylation_pct: Window methylation (%)

- component: table
  title: Binned methylation table
  description: |-
    Each row is a 10 kb window of a library, with its mean CpG methylation, the number of CpGs and the density class. It answers the exact value of a window.
    How to read: filter on a chromosome and sort by methylation to list extreme windows.

- component: figure
  title: PCR duplication per library
  description: |-
    Each bar is a library: the percentage of aligned reads removed as PCR duplicates. It answers which libraries were over-amplified relative to their complexity.
    How to read: libraries prepared alike should have similar rates. A library well above the others carries less unique information than its read count suggests, so weigh its methylation calls with care.
    Note: Bismark publishes no duplication cut-off. Deduplication is not recommended for RRBS, amplicon or other target-enrichment libraries, where duplicates are expected.
    Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median PCR duplication of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of Bismark.
    Source: https://felixkrueger.github.io/Bismark/usage/deduplication/
  visu_type: bar
  dict_kwargs:
    x: sample
    y: pct_duplication
    color: sample
    labels:
      sample: Library
      pct_duplication: PCR duplication (%)
  reference_lines:
  - axis: y
    stat: median
    column: pct_duplication

- component: card
  title: Average PCR duplication
  description: |-
    The hero number is the mean duplication percentage, and the box shows the spread across libraries. It answers how redundant the run is overall.
    How to read: a tight box means libraries share a similar complexity. A long upper whisker is a library to open in the bar chart.
  column: pct_duplication
  aggregation: average
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: Duplication rate, with its spread

- component: card
  title: Highest PCR duplication
  description: |-
    The hero number is the largest duplication percentage of any library, shown with the median and the lowest. It answers how far the worst library is from the rest.
    How to read: a maximum close to the median means no library stands out. A wide gap marks a library that was over-amplified.
    Note: Bismark publishes no duplication cut-off, so no pass mark is drawn.
    Source: https://felixkrueger.github.io/Bismark/usage/deduplication/
  column: pct_duplication
  aggregation: max
  aggregations:
  - median
  - min
  secondary_layout: compact
  caption: Highest library, with the median and the lowest

- component: card
  title: Alignments kept after deduplication
  description: |-
    The hero number is the total of alignments carried into methylation extraction, and the histogram shows how they spread over libraries. It answers how much usable depth remains.
    How to read: a library with far fewer kept alignments than its peers will contribute little to window-level methylation. Compare it with the duplication bar chart.
  column: leftover_sequences
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  - min
  secondary_layout: histogram
  caption: Alignments kept per library

- component: table
  title: Deduplication table
  description: |-
    Each row is a library with the alignments examined, the duplicates removed, the duplication percentage and the alignments left. It answers the exact counts behind the bar chart.
    How to read: sort by duplication to find the most redundant library.

- component: advanced_viz
  id: mbias_context_profile
  title: M-bias in every cytosine context
  description: |-
    Each line is one read of one library in one cytosine context (CpG, CHG or CHH): the percentage of methylated calls at each position along the read. It answers whether any part of a read is biased, and whether conversion fails at the read ends.
    How to read: CpG sits high and CHG and CHH sit near zero in most mammalian data. A line that bends at the read ends, such as the start of PBAT reads or the first bases of read 2 after end repair, shows a methylation bias at those positions, so ignore them during methylation extraction.
    Source: https://felixkrueger.github.io/Bismark/usage/methylation-extraction/ and https://felixkrueger.github.io/Bismark/faq/conversion-efficiency/
  kind: profile
  config:
    x_title: Position in read (bp)
    y_title: Methylation (%)
    legend_pos: bottom
  roles:
    series: series
    x: position
    y: pct_methylation

- component: card
  title: CHH methylation along reads
  description: |-
    The hero number is the mean methylation in the CHH context over all read positions, and the box shows how much positions differ. It answers how completely unmethylated cytosines were converted.
    How to read: values near zero mean good conversion. A high mean or a wide box points to non-conversion, often at the read start, so check the curve.
    Note: this reading assumes non-CG methylation is near zero, as in mammals. Other organisms can show real non-CG methylation.
    Source: https://felixkrueger.github.io/Bismark/faq/conversion-efficiency/
  column: pct_methylation
  aggregation: average
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  filter_expr: pl.col('context') == 'CHH'
  caption: CHH methylation along reads, with its spread

- component: card
  title: Methylation calls by context
  description: |-
    The hero number is the total of methylation calls counted in the M-bias tables, and the bars split it by cytosine context. It answers how much data sits behind each context.
    How to read: CHH and CHG usually hold far more calls than CpG because those contexts are more frequent in the genome.
  column: coverage
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: top_n
  breakdown_col: context
  top_n_count: 3
  caption: Calls, by context

- component: table
  title: M-bias table, all contexts
  description: |-
    Each row is a read position of one read of one library in one context, with its methylation percentage and the number of calls. It answers the exact value and the depth at each position.
    How to read: filter on a context and a read to follow one curve. A low call count at a position gives a noisy percentage.

- component: advanced_viz
  id: mbias_cpg_profile
  title: CpG M-bias curve
  description: |-
    Each line is one read of one library: the percentage of methylated CpG calls at each position along the read. It answers whether the first or last bases of a read carry a methylation bias.
    How to read: a flat line means methylation does not depend on the position. A line that rises or falls at the ends, typically at the start of read 2 or after end repair, marks bases that bias the calls. Ignore those positions during methylation extraction when the bias is clear.
    Source: https://felixkrueger.github.io/Bismark/usage/methylation-extraction/
  kind: profile
  config:
    x_title: Position in read (bp)
    y_title: CpG methylation (%)
    legend_pos: bottom
  roles:
    series: series
    x: position
    y: pct_methylation

- component: card
  title: CpG methylation along reads
  description: |-
    The hero number is the mean CpG methylation over all read positions, and the box shows how much the positions differ. It answers how stable methylation is along the read.
    How to read: a narrow box means little positional bias. A wide box or long whiskers point to the end positions seen in the curve.
  column: pct_methylation
  aggregation: average
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: Methylation along the read, with its spread

- component: table
  title: M-bias table
  description: |-
    Each row is a read position of one read of one library, with its CpG methylation percentage and the number of calls behind it. It answers the exact value and the depth at each position.
    How to read: a position with low coverage gives a noisy percentage, so check the coverage column before reading a spike.

- component: figure
  title: Methylation by cytosine context
  description: |-
    Each bar is the percentage of methylated cytosines of one library in one context (CpG, CHG or CHH). It answers whether CpG methylation is high and non-CpG methylation low, as bisulfite conversion should leave it.
    How to read: CpG methylation is high in most mammalian cells while CHG and CHH sit close to zero. A raised CHG or CHH bar means non-conversion, or real non-CG methylation in organisms that have it.
    Source: https://felixkrueger.github.io/Bismark/faq/conversion-efficiency/
  visu_type: bar
  dict_kwargs:
    x: sample
    y: pct_methylated
    color: context
    barmode: group
    labels:
      sample: Library
      pct_methylated: Methylated cytosines (%)
      context: Context

- component: card
  title: Average CpG methylation
  description: |-
    The hero number is the mean percentage of methylated cytosines in the CpG context, and the box shows the spread across libraries. It answers how methylated the libraries are overall.
    How to read: a tight box means comparable libraries. A library far from the others differs in biology, cell composition or conversion, so compare it with the PCA before drawing a conclusion.
  column: pct_methylated
  aggregation: average
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  filter_expr: pl.col('context') == 'CpG'
  caption: CpG methylation, with its spread

- component: card
  title: Highest CHH methylation
  description: |-
    The hero number is the largest CHH methylation percentage of any library, shown with the median and the lowest. It answers how incomplete bisulfite conversion could be at worst.
    How to read: a value of 0.3 percent means conversion was at least 99.7 percent efficient, so values near zero are good. A library well above its peers is the one to check first.
    Note: this reading assumes non-CG methylation is near zero, as in mammals. Bismark publishes no cut-off for it.
    Source: https://felixkrueger.github.io/Bismark/faq/conversion-efficiency/
  column: pct_methylated
  aggregation: max
  aggregations:
  - median
  - min
  secondary_layout: compact
  filter_expr: pl.col('context') == 'CHH'
  caption: Highest library, with the median and the lowest

- component: card
  title: Methylated calls by context
  description: |-
    The hero number is the total of methylated cytosine calls, and the bars split it by context. It answers where the methylated calls come from.
    How to read: CpG should carry most of the methylated calls in a mammalian library. A large CHH or CHG share would raise a conversion question.
  column: methylated_c
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: top_n
  breakdown_col: context
  top_n_count: 3
  caption: Methylated calls, by context

- component: table
  title: Methylation by context table
  description: |-
    Each row is a library in one context, with the methylated and unmethylated cytosine counts and the methylation percentage. It answers the exact counts behind the bar chart.
    How to read: filter on a context to compare libraries.

- component: advanced_viz
  id: density_profile
  title: Distribution of per-CpG methylation
  description: |-
    Each line is a library: the share of its CpGs that fall in each 2 percent methylation bin. It answers how methylation is distributed across individual CpGs.
    How to read: in most human cell types 70 to 80 percent of CpGs are methylated, so a main peak near 100 percent with a smaller one near 0 percent is expected. A library whose curve is flat, or whose peak near zero has drifted up, suggests incomplete conversion or too little depth for site calls.
    Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23925113/
  kind: profile
  config:
    x_title: CpG methylation (%)
    y_title: Share of CpGs (%)
    legend_pos: bottom
  roles:
    series: series
    x: methylation_bin
    y: fraction_of_cpgs

- component: card
  title: Tallest methylation peak
  description: |-
    The hero number is the largest share of CpGs found in a single bin of any library, shown with the median and upper quartile bin share. It answers how sharp the methylation peaks are.
    How to read: a tall peak means most CpGs of a library share one methylation level. Low peaks mean the methylation is spread out.
  column: fraction_of_cpgs
  aggregation: max
  aggregations:
  - median
  - q3
  secondary_layout: compact
  caption: Fullest bin, with the median and upper quartile bin

- component: card
  title: CpGs counted
  description: |-
    The hero number is the total of CpGs counted in the density bins, shown with the median and the largest bin. It answers how much data the densities rest on.
    How to read: a total far lower for one library means its density is noisier than the others.
  column: n_cpgs
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: compact
  caption: CpGs counted, with the median and fullest bin

- component: figure
  title: Per-CpG methylation density
  description: |-
    Each line is a library: the share of its CpGs in each 2 percent methylation bin. It answers how methylation is distributed across CpGs.
    How to read: compare the height of the peaks near 0 and near 100 percent between libraries. A library that departs from the others has a different methylome or a conversion problem.
    Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23925113/
  visu_type: line
  dict_kwargs:
    x: methylation_bin
    y: fraction_of_cpgs
    color: sample
    labels:
      methylation_bin: CpG methylation (%)
      fraction_of_cpgs: Share of CpGs (%)
      sample: Library

- component: table
  title: Methylation density table
  description: |-
    Each row is a methylation bin of one library, with the CpG count and the share of its CpGs. It answers the exact counts behind the density curves.
    How to read: filter on a library and sort by bin to follow its curve.

- component: card
  title: Reads through alignment
  description: |-
    The hero number is the total of reads sequenced, and the funnel shows how many aligned and how many remained after deduplication. It answers how much of the input became usable alignments.
    How to read: a narrow drop at each step is healthy. A large drop at alignment points to mapping problems, and a large drop at deduplication to over-amplification.
  column: total_reads
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  - min
  secondary_layout: attrition
  attrition_cols:
  - aligned_reads
  - unique_reads
  caption: Reads, from sequenced to aligned and unique

- component: card
  title: Lowest bisulfite conversion
  description: |-
    The hero number is the lowest bisulfite conversion efficiency of any library, read as 100 percent minus its CHH methylation, with the median and the best. It answers how complete the conversion was in the worst library.
    How to read: values near 100 percent are good, since few unmethylated cytosines remain unconverted. A library that stands out below the others inherits false methylation calls.
    Note: this reading assumes CHH methylation is near zero, as in mammals, and Bismark publishes no cut-off.
    Source: https://felixkrueger.github.io/Bismark/faq/conversion-efficiency/
  column: conversion_efficiency_pct
  aggregation: min
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: gauge
  coverage_max: 100.0
  caption: Weakest library, out of 100%

- component: card
  title: Average alignment yield
  description: |-
    The hero number is the mean percentage of reads that aligned, and the box shows the spread across libraries. It answers how well the run mapped.
    How to read: a tight box means libraries mapped alike. A long lower whisker is a library to check against the trimming and genome choice.
  column: pct_aligned
  aggregation: average
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: Alignment yield, with its spread

- component: card
  title: Average PCR duplication
  description: |-
    The hero number is the mean percentage of aligned reads removed as duplicates, and the box shows the spread. It answers how redundant the libraries are.
    How to read: a tight box means similar complexity. A library with a long upper whisker was over-amplified.
  column: pct_duplicate
  aggregation: average
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: Duplication rate, with its spread

- component: card
  title: Average CpG methylation
  description: |-
    The hero number is the mean CpG methylation percentage, and the box shows the spread across libraries. It answers how methylated the libraries are.
    How to read: a tight box means comparable libraries. A library far from the others differs in biology or conversion.
  column: pct_cpg_methylation
  aggregation: average
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: CpG methylation, with its spread

- component: card
  title: CpG calls
  description: |-
    The hero number is the total of CpG methylation calls, and the histogram shows how they spread over libraries. It answers how deep the methylation data is.
    How to read: a library with far fewer calls than its peers carries less evidence for window-level methylation.
  column: cpgs_called
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: histogram
  caption: CpG calls per library

- component: figure
  title: Bisulfite conversion per library
  description: |-
    Each bar is a library: its bisulfite conversion efficiency, read as 100 percent minus its CHH methylation. It answers whether every library converted completely.
    How to read: bars close to 100 percent mean few unmethylated cytosines remained unconverted. A shorter bar marks a library whose methylation calls may include false positives.
    Note: this reading assumes CHH methylation is near zero, as in mammals, and Bismark publishes no cut-off.
    Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median conversion efficiency of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of Bismark.
    Source: https://felixkrueger.github.io/Bismark/faq/conversion-efficiency/
  visu_type: bar
  dict_kwargs:
    x: sample
    y: conversion_efficiency_pct
    color: sample
    labels:
      sample: Library
      conversion_efficiency_pct: Conversion efficiency (%)
  reference_lines:
  - axis: y
    stat: median
    column: conversion_efficiency_pct

- component: table
  title: Run summary table
  description: |-
    Each row is a library with its read funnel, its cytosine counts per context and the ratios derived from them. It answers the exact numbers behind every card.
    How to read: sort by conversion or by alignment yield to find the weakest library.

- component: advanced_viz
  id: variable_windows_heatmap
  title: Most variable methylation windows
  description: |-
    Each cell is the mean CpG methylation of one of the most variable 10 kb windows (rows) in one library (columns), with the chromosome and the variance of each window as side annotations. It answers which regions differ most between libraries.
    How to read: libraries of one condition should share a colour pattern across the rows. A block of windows that flips between groups is a candidate region, and a library that follows the wrong group is an outlier to check.
    Note: this is a ranking by variance, not a test. The group comparison tab holds the statistics.
  kind: complex_heatmap
  config:
    row_annotation_cols:
    - chromosome
    - window_variance
  roles:
    index: window_id

- component: card
  title: Variance of the top windows
  description: |-
    The hero number is the largest methylation variance across libraries of any listed window, and the box shows the spread among them. It answers how strongly the top windows differ between libraries.
    How to read: a high maximum with a low median means a few windows dominate. A flat box means the ranking has no standout region.
  column: window_variance
  aggregation: max
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: Window variance, with its spread

- component: card
  title: Chromosomes of the top windows
  description: |-
    The hero number is how many chromosomes carry a listed window, with the count of windows beside it, and the bars rank the chromosomes by windows. It answers whether variable windows cluster on a few chromosomes.
    How to read: a chromosome far ahead of the others can mean a copy-number or sex difference between libraries rather than regulated methylation.
  column: chromosome
  aggregation: nunique
  aggregations:
  - count
  secondary_layout: top_n
  breakdown_col: chromosome
  top_n_count: 3
  caption: Chromosomes with the most variable windows

- component: table
  title: Most variable windows table
  description: |-
    Each row is a window with its chromosome, its variance and its methylation in every library. It answers the exact values behind the heatmap.
    How to read: sort by variance and compare the library columns.

- component: advanced_viz
  id: correlation_heatmap
  title: Library methylation correlation
  description: |-
    Each cell is the Pearson correlation between the window methylation of two libraries, computed over their shared 10 kb windows, with rows and columns clustered. It answers which libraries have the most similar methylomes.
    How to read: replicates of one condition should form blocks of high correlation. A library that clusters with the wrong block can be a sample swap, a mislabelled sheet or a conversion failure, so check the sample sheet and the conversion cards.
    Note: the diagonal is 1 by construction.
  kind: complex_heatmap
  roles:
    index: sample

- component: table
  title: Library correlation table
  description: |-
    Each row is a library with its correlation to every other library. It answers the exact value behind a cell of the heatmap.
    How to read: sort a column to find the library closest to or furthest from another.

- component: advanced_viz
  id: window_volcano
  title: Window methylation volcano
  description: |-
    Each point is a 10 kb window: the methylation difference between the two groups on the horizontal axis and its adjusted p-value on the vertical axis. It answers which regions differ most, in which direction and how confidently.
    How to read: windows in the upper left and right corners lose or gain methylation with the highest confidence. With only a handful of libraries per group this is a screen, so confirm any region in the genome view before acting.
    Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is an adjusted p-value of 0.05 (Benjamini-Hochberg) and the vertical lines are a difference of 10 percentage points. Both are the call rule of this table, set by the recipe, and not a published standard.
    Note: Bismark and nf-core/methylseq define no differential-methylation cut-off.
  kind: volcano
  config:
    significance_threshold: 0.05
    effect_threshold: 10.0
    top_n_labels: 8
    effect_label: Methylation difference (points)
    significance_label: -log10 adjusted p-value
  roles:
    feature_id: window_id
    effect_size: delta_methylation
    significance: padj
    label: window_id
    category: direction

- component: advanced_viz
  id: window_manhattan
  title: Window methylation Manhattan plot
  description: |-
    Each point is a 10 kb window along the genome, with the significance of its group difference (minus log10 of the adjusted p-value) as height and the call as colour. It answers where on the genome the differences concentrate.
    How to read: a cluster of tall points on one chromosome marks a region that loses or gains methylation as a block. Isolated points are weaker evidence, so check neighbouring windows.
    Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is minus log10 of 0.05, an adjusted p-value of 0.05. It is the call rule of this table, set by the recipe, and not a published standard.
  kind: manhattan
  config:
    score_threshold: 1.30103
    color_by_columns:
    - direction
    default_color_by: direction
    top_n_labels: 8
  roles:
    chr: chromosome
    pos: position
    score: neg_log10_padj
    feature: window_id
    effect: delta_methylation

- component: card
  title: Windows tested, by call
  description: |-
    The hero number is the count of windows tested, shown with the largest loss and gain in percentage points, and the ring splits them by call. It answers how many windows differ and in which direction.
    How to read: a ring almost entirely not significant means little difference between the groups. A lopsided ring shows a global shift in one direction.
    Note: the calls follow the recipe rule of an adjusted p-value below 0.05 and a difference of at least 10 percentage points, not a published standard.
  column: delta_methylation
  aggregation: count
  aggregations:
  - min
  - max
  secondary_layout: donut
  breakdown_col: direction
  caption: Windows, by call

- component: card
  title: Methylation gains
  description: |-
    The hero number is the largest methylation gain among the hypermethylated windows, and the box shows the spread of the gains. It answers how large the gains are.
    How to read: a box close to the 10 point rule means gains are modest. A long upper whisker marks a few windows with a large change.
    Note: the 10 point rule is the call rule of this table, not a published standard.
  column: delta_methylation
  aggregation: max
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  filter_expr: pl.col('direction') == 'Hypermethylated'
  caption: Gains, with their spread

- component: card
  title: Methylation losses
  description: |-
    The hero number is the largest methylation loss among the hypomethylated windows, and the box shows the spread of the losses. It answers how large the losses are.
    How to read: a box close to the 10 point rule means losses are modest. A long lower whisker marks a few windows with a large change.
    Note: the 10 point rule is the call rule of this table, not a published standard.
  column: delta_methylation
  aggregation: min
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  filter_expr: pl.col('direction') == 'Hypomethylated'
  caption: Losses, with their spread

- component: card
  title: Chromosomes carrying calls
  description: |-
    The hero number is how many chromosomes carry a called window, with the count of called windows beside it, and the bars rank the chromosomes. It answers whether the calls cluster on a few chromosomes.
    How to read: a chromosome far ahead of the others can reflect a copy-number or sex difference between the groups rather than regulated methylation.
  column: chromosome
  aggregation: nunique
  aggregations:
  - count
  secondary_layout: top_n
  breakdown_col: chromosome
  top_n_count: 3
  filter_expr: pl.col('direction') != 'Not significant'
  caption: Chromosomes with the most calls

- component: card
  title: Strongest window significance
  description: |-
    The hero number is the largest minus log10 adjusted p-value, and the histogram shows how significance spreads over windows. It answers how strong the best window is and how many windows stand out.
    How to read: a histogram piled near zero with a thin tail is a screen with few real differences. Open the volcano to see the tail windows.
  column: neg_log10_padj
  aggregation: max
  aggregations:
  - median
  - q3
  secondary_layout: histogram
  caption: Significance, window by window

- component: figure
  title: Distribution of methylation differences
  description: |-
    Each bar counts windows in a bin of methylation difference between the two groups, split by call. It answers how the called windows sit in the overall distribution.
    How to read: a distribution centred on zero is expected when the groups are alike. A shifted centre suggests a global difference or a batch effect.
    Lines and annotations: the call colours use an adjusted p-value below 0.05 and a difference of at least 10 percentage points, the call rule of this table and not a published standard.
  visu_type: histogram
  dict_kwargs:
    x: delta_methylation
    color: direction
    labels:
      delta_methylation: Methylation difference (percentage points)
      direction: Call

- component: table
  title: Window comparison table
  description: |-
    Each row is a 10 kb window with the two group means, the difference, the test statistic, the adjusted p-value and the call. It answers the exact statistics of any window.
    How to read: sort by adjusted p-value to list the best windows, then select a row to inspect it in the other tiles.
  row_selection_enabled: true
  row_selection_column: window_id

- component: advanced_viz
  id: pca_embedding
  title: Libraries on the binned methylome
  description: |-
    Each point is a library, placed by its methylation over the 10 kb windows on the first principal components. It answers whether libraries separate by the design of the experiment or by depth, batch or conversion.
    How to read: replicates should sit close together and conditions apart. A library that sits alone, or a split that follows a technical factor, is a batch or quality effect to investigate before any comparison.
    Note: the components are computed on the run's windows only, so axes have no absolute meaning across runs.
  kind: embedding
  config:
    axis_prefix: PC
  roles:
    sample_id: sample_id
    dim_1: dim_1
    dim_2: dim_2
    dim_3: dim_3

- component: figure
  title: First two components
  description: |-
    Each point is a library on the first two principal components of its binned methylome. It answers how libraries relate on the two axes of largest variation.
    How to read: neighbouring points are similar libraries. Hover a point to read the library, and compare with the correlation heatmap for the same structure.
  visu_type: scatter
  dict_kwargs:
    x: dim_1
    y: dim_2
    hover_name: sample_id
    labels:
      dim_1: PC1
      dim_2: PC2

- component: table
  title: PCA table
  description: |-
    Each row is a library with its coordinates on the first components and the design columns. It answers the exact position of each point.
    How to read: sort by a component to find the libraries at the extremes.
